In four US national surveys of psychiatric disorders, most people who had ever met the criteria for drug dependence had not met them in the past year: 76% in the National Comorbidity Survey (1990–92), 83% in its replication (2001–03) and 81% in the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions (2001–02), against 57% in the Epidemiologic Catchment Area survey (1980–84), which combined abuse with dependence and counted remission only when no symptoms remained, where the later surveys accepted two or fewer dependence symptoms (Heyman, 2013, the reviewer's own calculation from the surveys' published lifetime and past-year figures, without intervals). Remission meant not meeting the criteria in the past year, not quitting: a person counted as remitted could relapse the next year, and in the 2001–02 survey's analyses by drug it was counted one drug at a time, so a person in remission from cocaine dependence could be dependent on another drug (people who had remitted but met the criteria again at the interview were not counted as remitted). In those analyses, counted from the recalled start of dependence, half of the people ever dependent on cocaine had remitted by about year 4, on cannabis by about year 6 (year 7 elsewhere in the same review), on alcohol by year 16 and on cigarettes by about year 30; ten years after the start of dependence 79%, 69%, 40% and 20% had remitted, while 5% of people dependent on cocaine remained dependent for at least 23 years and 5% of those dependent on cannabis for at least 36; heroin and other opioids are not among the drugs analysed (Heyman, 2013, from the survey's published curves and yearly figures its authors supplied). set.plain: Do people recover from drug or alcohol problems, even without treatment? Many do, but the numbers depend on how studies count. In US national surveys, about 8 in 10 people who had ever been dependent on a drug had not met the criteria in the past year (57 in 100 in an older survey with a stricter rule). That is not the same as quitting: people could still use, could relapse later, and in the figures by drug could be dependent on another drug. By drug, half of the people ever dependent on cocaine had recovered within about 4 years of becoming dependent, on cannabis about 6, alcohol 16 and cigarettes about 30, though some stayed dependent for decades; heroin was not among these drugs. Few people with current dependence were in treatment. Of US soldiers addicted to narcotics in Vietnam, 5 in 100 were addicted again in their first year home and 12 in 100 within 3 years, and few entered drug treatment after coming home. In a US survey, about 64 in 100 adults with alcohol dependence no longer had enough signs to count as dependent three years later, though some still had a few. In 20 long studies, mostly of people who had been in treatment, and one survey, 35 to 54 in 100 were in recovery when last seen, on average 17 years later. For alcohol, studies of recovery without treatment give anything from about 3 to 98 in 100, mostly because they count different groups: among people who have recovered, many were never treated; among everyone with a drinking problem, fewer recover without treatment in a given year.
set.population: US adults in four national surveys of psychiatric disorders (Epidemiologic Catchment Area 1980–84, nearly 20,000 people in five metropolitan areas, prisons included; National Comorbidity Survey 1990–92, about 8,100; its replication 2001–03, about 9,200; NESARC 2001–02, about 43,000), as recalculated in a review (Heyman, 2013); US Army enlisted men returning from Vietnam in September 1971, interviewed 8 to 12 months later (451 in a random general sample; 898 in both samples) (Robins et al., 1975) and about 3 years after return (Robins, 1993); US adults in a national household survey interviewed in 2001–2002 and 2004–2005 (34,653 re-interviewed; 1,172 of them with past-year alcohol dependence at the first interview, an editors' sum) (Vergés et al., 2012); 21 studies of people with alcohol, heroin or several-drug use disorders published 2000–2015 (20 cohorts, 15 recruited through treatment, and one national survey's lifetime estimate) (Fleury et al., 2016); 27 studies of untreated remission from alcohol problems, 1976–2018, mostly North American (Mellor et al., 2019)
set.exposure: Having had an alcohol or drug problem (DSM drug dependence as each survey diagnosed it, with abuse and dependence combined in the oldest survey; dependence on cocaine, cannabis, alcohol or cigarettes, drug by drug; narcotic dependence or addiction in Vietnam, self-reported or by the study's own criteria; DSM-IV alcohol dependence; substance use disorders as each cohort diagnosed them; alcohol problems as each study defined them), with or without treatment as each study defined it
set.outcome: No longer meeting the criteria for the problem (remission) at a later interview or at the last follow-up, as each study defined it (not meeting dependence criteria in the past year, meaning two or fewer dependence symptoms, or no symptoms in the oldest survey; time from the start of dependence to remission, drug by drug; not dependent again within about a year, and not addicted again within 3 years, in the Vietnam veterans; not meeting full DSM-IV criteria in the year before an interview about three years later; at least six months without meeting criteria; abstinence or moderate drinking), and the share of it without treatment

grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: The figures on recovery without treatment are second-hand from a review that did not appraise its 27 studies, 71 of whose 124 estimates the reviewers calculated themselves (card sc_mellor_2019: narrative-review checklist, high); the meta-analysis reports no appraisal of its cohorts and pools follow-ups of 3 to 50 years with a lifetime survey estimate (card sc_fleury_2016: AMSTAR 2 critically low); the figures for drug dependence in the US surveys are a reviewer's own calculations from published prevalences and from curves and unpublished yearly figures the survey's authors supplied, without intervals, from single interviews that miss people in jails and prisons and people who had died (card sc_heyman_2013: narrative-review checklist, high); the Vietnam study rests on self-report, study-specific criteria, a window of about a year in its first report and a 95% figure without a denominator (card sc_robins_1975: JBI moderate), and its three-year and treatment figures come from the principal investigator's lecture, which gives no denominators or definitions and whose text and graphs disagree in places (card sc_robins_1993: narrative-review checklist, high); in the national survey of alcohol dependence, offset includes people with residual symptoms and 20% were not re-interviewed (card sc_verges_2012). A claim seen through reviews is downgraded for risk of bias (METHODS 6.3).

grade.domains.inconsistency.note: Estimates range from 2.7% to 98.3%, but the alcohol review shows that the range follows mostly from the denominator and the definitions, and every source finds remission common on its own terms; the four US surveys agree closely (76% to 83% under the same rule, 57% under a stricter one). Not downgraded, because the statement ties each figure to its definition and sample.

grade.domains.indirectness.note: Rated as worded: each figure is given with its population (US adults in national surveys, 1980–2003; young US enlisted men in 1971–1974; US adults with alcohol dependence in 2001–2005; mostly treatment-recruited cohorts; mostly North American alcohol studies); the statement says that remission meant not meeting the criteria in the past year, not quitting, and was counted drug by drug in the analyses by drug, that heroin and other opioids are not among the drugs in those analyses, and that no source read counted recovery without treatment for drugs other than alcohol.

grade.domains.imprecision.note: Large samples behind the survey figures (no intervals printed); the Vietnam figures for dependence after return rest on small numbers (about 4 to 5 men dependent after return in the general sample) and approximate readings of a figure, stated as such.

set.grade.reasoning: Descriptive claim: starts low and is rated as a description of the samples. Down one for risk of bias, because the part of the question about recovery without treatment rests on second-hand, unappraised estimates (and on a meta-analysis of unappraised, mostly treatment-recruited cohorts), and the survey figures for drugs are a reviewer's recalculations: very low. A lenient reading would rate the Vietnam and national-survey figures alone (primary data from a near-complete random sample and weighted national surveys) as low for the narrower statement that many people no longer meet the criteria within one to three years; the rating is set by the weakest necessary link. Not upgraded (descriptive). Status replicated: the direction holds in independent samples (the Vietnam veterans; the US national surveys; the cohorts pooled by Fleury et al.), but the 2001–02 US survey (NESARC) appears in several places: Heyman's survey figure and his curves by drug, which come from the same remission analysis (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011, in Addiction) that Fleury et al. pooled as their lifetime estimate; Vergés et al.; Moss et al. (2010), a general-population sample from the same survey followed for three years, in Fleury et al.; and Dawson et al. in Mellor et al.; these are not counted as independent of each other, and the Vietnam cohort's 1975 report and 1993 lecture are one study. Not used: Heyman's comparison of treated and untreated Vietnam veterans, which joins figures for different groups and time spans; his conclusions that remission does not require treatment and that most people stop by about age 30, which go beyond what the surveys measured; the 95% remission rate as a figure (no stated denominator), Fleury et al.'s annual remission rates (inconsistent with its pooled proportions), its 14 years of use before remission (not derivable from its table) and its conservative-rate comparison by treatment at entry (not reproducible from its study values), and Mellor et al.'s medians as rates (card reporting issues). The comparison of cohorts by treatment at entry describes who entered each study, not who recovered without treatment, and the low share of people in treatment in the surveys describes current cases, not who recovered without it.
